name: Sciton BBL / Moxi / Halo
lead: BBL, Moxi and Halo are treatments performed on laser and light platforms made by Sciton. BBL (BroadBand Light) is an intense pulsed light treatment, Moxi is a fractionated 1927-nm laser, and Halo is a dual-wavelength 2940/1470-nm hybrid fractional laser, as described by the titles of registered studies.[1][2] They are used for photoaging, pigment, redness, texture and scars, and are sometimes combined in one session.[1]

Evidence is a mix of small studies. A completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for skin pigment[1], a split-face study compared IPL with pulsed dye laser for facial erythema[3], and a 2023 study examined fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes.[4] Many older Sciton papers concern erbium:YAG resurfacing.

paras: BBL is a broadband, non-laser light source of the intense pulsed light type, which uses filtered flashlamp light to target pigment or blood vessels.[5] A split-face comparison found IPL could be used in place of pulsed dye laser for reducing facial erythema.[3]

Moxi is described in registered studies as a fractionated 1927-nm laser for pigmentation and photodamage.[1][4] Fractionated resurfacing treats a pattern of microscopic columns and leaves surrounding skin intact.
Halo is described as a dual-wavelength 2940/1470 nm hybrid fractional laser.[1][6] A recruiting trial evaluates a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in patients with skin of colour.[6]

Studies of ablative erbium and CO2 resurfacing report differences in healing time and side-effect rates, and trials of wound dressings after fractional erbium resurfacing show post-procedure care is an active area of study.[7][8] Laser-induced hyperpigmentation is listed as a condition in one registered trial.[6]

A completed 15-participant trial combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for pigment (NCT06091215), a 38-participant phase 4 trial examined a moisturiser with a non-ablative laser for photoaging, and a 5-participant study evaluated infrared and broadband light for skin ageing.[1][9][10] A study of fractionated 1927-nm laser reported on diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes.[4] Single-pass CO2 and multiple-pass Er:YAG resurfacing were directly compared for healing and side effects in an older trial.[7] Sample sizes are small and registry entries here do not summarise results.

card.aka: BBL, BroadBand Light, Moxi, Halo, BBL Hero
card.note: Professional treatments; evidence is mostly small pilots.

quick.overview:
BBL, Moxi and Halo are three treatments run on Sciton platforms: broadband light, a light fractional 1927-nm laser and a deeper hybrid fractional laser. Clinics sometimes combine them for pigment, texture and photoaging.

Published work naming them is small, mostly pilot studies and trials with a few dozen participants.
quick.mechanism: BBL uses filtered flashlamp light on pigment and vessels. Moxi and Halo create tiny columns of controlled injury so skin remodels.
quick.risks: Listed concerns include pigment change after laser, healing time with deeper resurfacing, and that these are clinic-only procedures.
